body: Stock market sector rotation: Energy leads while communication services suffers a sharp decline U.S. stock market leadership is becoming increasingly selective. Three trading sessions reveal important differences between sectors, and even between industries within the same sector. U.S. stocks are showing a notable change in leadership. Between the October 20 and October 23, 2026 closes, the Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE) gained 2.00%, while the Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLC) fell 4.25%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) declined 1.18% over the same period. For stock investors and traders, the message is not simply that the market is falling. Some sectors are attracting buying interest while others are struggling, and these differences may help identify where the next opportunities and risks develop. What the latest sector performance tells us Energy was the strongest of the 11 major U.S. stock market sectors over the three sessions, followed by utilities, which gained 1.62%. Consumer staples, real estate, financials and materials also finished higher. Together, these six sectors outperformed a declining S&P 500 benchmark. The weakest performances came from communication services, consumer discretionary stocks, industrials and technology. The particularly interesting development is the gap between the leaders and laggards. Energy outperformed communication services by 6.25 percentage points in just three sessions.

Trading on Margin: What It Means and How to Get Started
body: Why trade Bitcoin if stocks can double? The leverage question traders miss A trader recently asked: "Why trade Bitcoin? What's it gonna do, 2x, 3x? These days stocks can do that. So what's the point?" It's a reasonable question, but it misses something fundamental about trading: leverage. Traders don't necessarily need Bitcoin, gold or a stock to double in price to achieve a substantial percentage return on their trading capital. Depending on the financial instrument and the size of their position, even a relatively small price movement can have a significant impact on their account. Unfortunately, that works in both directions. Leverage can accelerate profits, but it can also destroy a trading account surprisingly quickly. Understanding how it works is one of the most important lessons in financial markets. What is leverage in trading? Leverage allows you to control a position worth more than the capital you commit to it. Imagine you have $10,000 available for trading and expect Bitcoin to rise by 3%. Without leverage (1x) You purchase $10,000 worth of Bitcoin. If BTC rises 3%, your position gains $300, representing a 3% return on your capital. If Bitcoin falls 3%, you lose $300 instead. With 5x leverage You use that same $10,000 as collateral to control a $50,000 Bitcoin position. A 3% rise now generates a $1,500 profit, equivalent to 15% of your starting capital. But a 3% decline produces a $1,500 loss, also 15% of your capital.
